source.authors: Alexei N. Skorobogatov and Efthymios Sofos

summary: Skorobogatov and Sofos prove Schinzel's Hypothesis (H) for 100% of n-tuples of integer polynomials of fixed degrees ordered by height: an averaged Bateman–Horn estimate (Theorem 1.9) by Linnik's dispersion method, with two-point prime correlations over coefficient boxes from Davenport's Möbius cancellation (§3) and local densities from a Bernoulli model (§2). They deduce density-one Hasse principles for cyclic norm equations N(z) = P(t) and diagonal conic bundles, and a 56% lower bound for x² + y² = f(t) (§§5–7). 103 items (6 library, 6 planned, 91 missing) are routed to two proposed Part IIs (Schinzel averages; random fibrations) and to ArithmeticStatistics ST.0, AnalyticNumberTheory AN.2/AN.5, ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.0, SieveMethodsAndPrimePatterns SV.2/SV.4 and HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions RP.2. Twenty-two findings are recorded. The main one: Lemma 3.14 is false for positive primes (E1), and the von Mangoldt function must be even on ℤ (E4); the proofs establish the both-sign forms, and the main theorems survive through the von Mangoldt count and a bound on negative values that uses A₁ > n. Reviewed by REV-PAPER-SKOROBOGATOV-SOFOS-23 (Claude Code, cc-2aeb03) and corrected in place: 149 items (7 library, 10 planned, 132 missing). 42 mistakes are recorded (26 misprints, 11 gaps, 5 errors; 5 reach a stated result, 8 a proof). Lemmas 3.14 and 4.9 are false as printed because they count only positive prime values (E1, E30); read with Λ even on ℤ they hold, and Theorems 1.1–1.5 and 1.9 stand; Corollary 1.10 and the square case of Corollary 1.7 are unproved as printed. Not formalised.

items.name: Fixed-degree coefficient box and height
items.statement: Let d_1,…,d_n be positive integers. The height |P| of P∈ℤ[t] is the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients; for P=(P_1,…,P_n)∈(ℤ[t])^n, |P|=max_i|P_i|. P>0 means the leading coefficient of P is positive. Fix integers n₀ and M and polynomials Q_i(t)∈ℤ[t] of degree at most d_i (i=1,…,n) such that ∏_{i=1}^n Q_i(n₀) and M are coprime. For H≥1, Poly(H):={P∈(ℤ[t])^n : |P|≤H, deg(P_i)=d_i, P_i>0, P_i≡Q_i (mod M) for i=1,…,n} (congruence coefficientwise, i.e. P_i−Q_i∈Mℤ[t]).
items.locator: §1 p. 677 (standing assumptions and definition of Poly(H), just before the subsection 'The least prime represented by a polynomial'); height of a polynomial p. 674 (before Theorem 1.1); height |P| of an n-tuple p. 675
items.note: Mathematical planning contract, not a claim of formalization; source issues and completion gates apply.

items.name: Schinzel tuple
items.statement: P=(P_1,…,P_n)∈(ℤ[t])^n is a Schinzel n-tuple if for every prime ℓ the reduction modulo ℓ of P_1(t)⋯P_n(t) is not divisible by t^ℓ−t, and the leading coefficient of each P_i is positive; equivalently (p. 677) Z_{P_1⋯P_n}(ℓ)≠ℓ for all primes ℓ and P_i>0 for all i, i.e. for each ℓ a single a∈𝔽_ℓ with ∏_iP_i(a)≠0. items.name: Schinzel on average in a congruence family
items.statement: Printed Theorem 1.2: Let d_1,…,d_n be positive integers. Fix integers n₀ and M. Assume we are given Q_1(t),…,Q_n(t) in ℤ[t] such that ∏_{i=1}^nQ_i(n₀) and M are coprime, and deg(Q_i(t))≤d_i for i=1,…,n. (Precise sense of 100%: Theorem 1.5. M≥1 is the implicit convention for a modulus.)

items.name: Pointwise averaged Bateman–Horn corollary
items.statement: Printed Corollary 1.10 (for reference; see E11): Let d be a positive integer. Fix any c∈ℝ with 0<c<1/2 and any A_1,A_2∈ℝ with 1<A_1<A_2. Then for all irreducible P∈ℤ[t], P>0, with deg(P)=d and all x with (log|P|)^{A_1}<x≤(log|P|)^{A_2} we have Σ_{m∈ℕ∩[1,x], P(m) prime} log P(m) = (∏_{ℓ prime, ℓ≤log x}(1−ℓ^{−1}Z_P(ℓ))/(1−ℓ^{−1}))·x + O(x/(log x)^c), with the exception of at most O(H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2}) of polynomials P such that |P|≤H. Proved form (Theorem 1.9 with n=M=n₀=1 plus Markov): for each fixed x, #{P: P>0, deg P=d, |P|≤H, (log|P|)^{A_1}<x≤(log|P|)^{A_2}, |θ_P(x)−𝔖_P(x)x|>x/(log x)^c} ≪ H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2}. Irreducibility is not needed. For the |P|-dependent range, split |P| dyadically and apply Theorem 1.9 at each dyadic height H_k with some A_1'∈(1,A_1).

items.name: Bernoulli nonvanishing variables
items.statement: For m ∈ F_ℓ, Y_m(P) = 1 if P(m) ≠ 0 and 0 otherwise (P ∈ Ω(d)); Y_m = χ(P(m)) with χ the principal character. On Ω = Ω(d1)×…×Ω(dn) with the product measure (2.2), X_m = 1 if ∏_i P_i(m) ≠ 0 and 0 otherwise, so X_m = ∏_i Y_m(P_i) and X_1+…+X_ℓ = ℓ − Z_{P1⋯Pn}(ℓ) (2.3). Lemma 2.1: the Y_m, m ∈ J, are independent whenever ♯J ≤ d+1; Lemma 2.3: the X_m are pairwise independent (all d_i ≥ 1, as d_i ∈ ℕ).

items.statement: Let K/ℚ be cyclic with character χ, S the set of primes ramified in K, and (P_1(t,m_1),…,P_n(t,m_n)) a Schinzel n-tuple. items.name: Second moment of the local Euler factor (Lemma 2.6) and first-moment identity
items.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ, d_1,…,d_n ∈ ℕ (so d_i ≥ 1), d = Σd_i, ℓ prime. Then ℓ^{−(d+n)} Σ_{P_i∈F_ℓ[t], deg P_i ≤ d_i} (1 − Z_{P1⋯Pn}(ℓ)/ℓ)² = γ_n(ℓ)(1 − 1/ℓ)^{2n}, with γ_n(ℓ) = 1 − 1/ℓ + ℓ^{n−1}/(ℓ−1)^n. Also (unnumbered, the first moment) ℓ^{−(d+n)} Σ_{deg P_i ≤ d_i} (1 − Z_{P1⋯Pn}(ℓ)/ℓ) = (1 − 1/ℓ)^n.
items.locator: Published Lemma 2.6 and the display after it, §2.2 p. 687
items.note: The proof writes the left side as ℓ^{−2}E[(ΣX_m)²] and uses Lemmas 2.2–2.3; the first moment uses only Lemma 2.2. Item 22 carries the content under kind 'definition', but no theorem item cites Lemma 2.6, which §4 uses. Brute-force check for ℓ ∈ {2,3,5} and (d_i) ∈ {(1),(2),(3),(1,1),(1,2)}: exact. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Uniform bound for the exponential sum of E_z over the value range (3.3)
items.statement: Fix d ≥ 1, δ1 ∈ (0,1), δ2 > 0. For H^{δ1} ≤ z ≤ H, natural numbers k, m ≤ (log H)^{δ2}, 𝓜 = max{k,m}, and every C > 0: ‖S_{E_z}‖_∞ ≪_C 𝓜^d H (log H)(log z)^{−C} ≪_{C,δ1} H (log H)^{1+dδ2−C}, where S_{E_z}(α) = Σ_{|c|≤(d+1)𝓜^d H} E_z(c)e^{icα}. The same holds with 𝓜 = k (one point), as used in Lemma 3.9.
items.locator: Published Eq. (3.3), proof of Proposition 3.8 p. 694; reused in the proof of Lemma 3.9 p. 695
items.note: Numbered and cited later ('Using (3.3) to bound S_{E_z}', p. 695). It follows from Corollary 3.3 only with the even convention Λ(n) = Λ(|n|), Λ(0) = 0: Corollary 3.3 bounds the c > 0 half, evenness gives the c < 0 half, and the c = 0 term |E_z(0)| = |Σ_{d≤z}μ(d)log d| ≪ z(log z)^{−C} is added (E4). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Pointwise and mean bounds for Λ_z and E_z
items.statement: For f ∈ {Λ_z, E_z} and t ∈ ℕ: |f(t)| ≤ Σ_{m|t} log m ≤ τ(t) log t. Hence Σ_{t≤y} |f(t)| ≪ y(log y)², and, for natural k, m ≤ (log H)^{δ2} and 𝓜 = max{k,m}, S_{|f|}(0) = Σ_{|c|≤(d+1)𝓜^d H} |f(c)| ≪ H(log H)²𝓜^d ≪ H(log H)^{2+dδ2}.
items.note: It uses the classical black box Σ_{t≤y} τ(t) ≪ y log y (Dirichlet), which the paper does not cite. With Λ even the bound applies to c < 0 through |c|. The c = 0 term needs |Λ_z(0)| ≤ Σ_{d≤z} log d ≤ z log z ≤ H log H and |E_z(0)| ≤ z log z, which still fit the stated bound (E4). The printed 'log t' for t ≤ 0 is meaningless. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Coefficient-box count with local conditions (CRT)
items.statement: For q ∈ ℕ, a ∈ Z and an interval I ⊂ ℝ of length L, ♯{c ∈ Z ∩ I : c ≡ a mod q} = L/q + O(1). Consequently, for W squarefree and coprime to M, and sets S_ℓ ⊆ Ω_ℓ(d_1)×…×Ω_ℓ(d_n) for ℓ | W: ♯{P ∈ Poly(H) : P mod ℓ ∈ S_ℓ for all ℓ | W} = 2^{−n}(2H/(WM) + O(1))^{d+n} ∏_{ℓ|W} ♯S_ℓ, with an absolute O(1) inside the power.
items.locator: Published proof of Proposition 2.8 p. 689 ('by the Chinese remainder theorem applied to the coefficients')
items.note: This is the finite CRT count behind K(H). With S_ℓ = T_ℓ and W ≤ H^{1/2} it gives K(H) = 2^d(H/M)^{d+n}∏_{ℓ|W}(1−c_ℓ) + O(H^{d+n−1/2}). The same count recurs in Lemma 3.10, p. 697. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: One-point coefficient Fourier identity in a residue class
items.statement: For d ≥ 1, k, Ω ∈ ℕ, R = Σ_{j=0}^d r_j t^j with 0 ≤ r_j < Ω, and f : Z → R, with S_f truncated at |c| ≤ (d+1)k^d H: Σ_{P>0, |P|≤H, deg P=d, P≡R mod Ω} f(P(k)) = (2π)^{−1} ∫_{−π}^{π} conj(S_f(α)) (Σ_{0<c_d≤H, c_d≡r_d (Ω)} e^{ic_d k^d α}) ∏_{j=0}^{d−1} (Σ_{|c_j|≤H, c_j≡r_j (Ω)} e^{ic_j k^j α}) dα.
items.locator: Published proof of Lemma 3.9 p. 695 (the display after 'Using that Λ − Λ_z = E_z…', corrected as in E7)
items.note: It is the one-variable analogue of Lemma 3.4 in a progression, applied with f = E_z. The printed display omits the integral and the factor conj(S_{E_z}) (E7), so the identity has no correct statement anywhere in the paper. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Dispersion expansion (4.1)
items.statement: Removing the condition P_i ≡ Q_i (mod M) can only increase ♯Poly(H)·V(x,H), so ♯Poly(H)V(x,H) ≤ Σ_P θ_P(x)² − 2x Σ_P 𝔖_P(x)θ_P(x) + x² Σ_P 𝔖_P(x)², all three sums over P ∈ ℤ[t]^n with |P| ≤ H, deg P_i = d_i, P_i > 0. Section 4 proves V(x,H) ≪ x²/log x from this, and Theorem 1.9 follows from R(x,H)² ≤ V(x,H).
items.note: Valid because each (θ_P − 𝔖_P x)² ≥ 0. Used in §4.4 (p. 714). Only an upper bound for Σθ² and a lower bound for Σ𝔖θ are needed, which is why E10 is harmless and E1 is repairable. The printed target 'x²/(log x)^{−1}' is E9. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Wintner's mean-value theorem (Iwaniec–Kowalski (1.72))
items.statement: For any arithmetic function g and any monotonic bounded h: [0,∞) → ℝ, for all x ≥ 1: Σ_{t≤x}(g∗h)(t) = ∫_0^x (Σ_{t≤y} (g(t)/t) h(y/t)) dy + O(Σ_{t≤x}|g(t)|), where g∗h is the Dirichlet convolution (h restricted to ℕ) and the implied constant depends on sup|h|.
items.locator: (4.2), proof of Lemma 4.3 p. 705, citing [39, Eq. (1.72)]
items.note: Cited black box. Used only with h ≡ 1 and g(t) = |μ(t)|∏_{p|t}((1+f(p))^n − 1), where it is elementary (Σ_{t≤x}(g∗1)(t) = Σ_{t≤x} g(t)⌊x/t⌋). I checked the displayed form is correct (Σ_{b≤Y}h(b) = ∫_0^Y h + O(sup|h|) for monotone h; replacing Σ_{t≤x} by Σ_{t≤y} inside the integral costs O(sup|h|Σ|g|)); I did not check the wording in Iwaniec–Kowalski. Missing: routed to route 4.

items.name: Second moment of θ_P with truncated singular product (4.5)
items.statement: Fix δ > 0. For 1 ≤ x ≤ (log H)^δ: Σ_{P∈ℤ[t]^n, |P|≤H, deg P_i=d_i, P_i>0} θ_P(x)² = (x² M^{n−2}/φ(M)^n) 2^d H^{d+n} ∏_{ℓ∤M, ℓ≤log x} γ_n(ℓ) + O(x²H^{d+n}/log x + xH^{d+n}(log H)^n).
items.note: Used in §4.4 (p. 714) together with Lemmas 4.7 and 4.9. As an equality for θ_P it inherits E10 (the printed proof gives only the upper bound; it is exact for θ^Λ); the dispersion needs only the upper bound. The x^{3/2}H^{d+n} term of Lemma 4.4 is absorbed since x^{1/2} ≥ log x. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Normalized truncated local product B_P(x)
items.statement: For P ∈ ℤ[t]^n (or R ∈ ((ℤ/W)[t])^n), x ≥ 1 and M ∈ ℕ put B_P(x) := ∏_{ℓ prime, ℓ∤M, ℓ ≤ log x} (1 − ℓ^{−1}Z_{P_1⋯P_n}(ℓ))/(1 − ℓ^{−1})^n. Then S_P(x) = 1(gcd(M, ∏P_i(n_0)) = 1)·M^{n−1}φ(M)^{−n}·B_P(x). Moreover B_P(x) = B_R(x) when R_i is the reduction of P_i modulo W = ∏_{ℓ∤M, ℓ≤log x} ℓ, since Z_P(ℓ) depends only on P mod ℓ.
items.note: Used in the proofs of Lemmas 4.7 and 4.9, and in the bound max_P S_P(x) in item 47. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Upper bound for the truncated singular series
items.statement: For x ≥ 1, n, M ∈ ℕ and every P (or R mod W): 0 ≤ B_P(x) ≤ ∏_{ℓ ≤ log x}(1 − ℓ^{−1})^{−n} ≪_n max(1, log log x)^n. Hence 0 ≤ S_P(x) ≪_{n,M} max(1, log log x)^n, uniformly in P.
items.note: Follows from 0 ≤ Z ≤ ℓ and Mertens (item 50). Gives the error term of Lemma 4.9 (Σ_R B_R ≤ W^{d+n}(log log x)^n) and the factor max_P S_P(x) in item 47. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Counting box polynomials in a coefficientwise residue class
items.statement: For d_i ≥ 1, H ≥ 1, q ∈ ℕ and F ∈ (ℤ/q)[t] with deg F ≤ d_i: #{P ∈ ℤ[t]: deg P = d_i, P > 0, |P| ≤ H, P ≡ F (mod q) coefficientwise} = 2^{d_i}H^{d_i+1}q^{−d_i−1} + O_{d_i}(1 + (H/q)^{d_i}). (The leading coefficient runs through an AP in (0, H]; the other d_i coefficients run through APs in [−H, H].)
items.note: Applied with q = k_iW, where k_i | M and gcd(k_i, W) = 1 (CRT). Since W ≤ x² ≤ H^{1/2}, summing over the k_i^{d_i} classes F_i gives relative error O_M(H^{−1/2}). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Möbius detection of the unit condition at n_0
items.statement: For M ∈ ℕ and a ∈ ℤ: Σ_{k | M, k | a} μ(k) = 1(gcd(M, a) = 1), and Σ_{k | M} μ(k)/k = φ(M)/M. For k | M, n_0 ∈ ℤ and d_i ≥ 0: #{F ∈ (ℤ/k)[t]: deg F ≤ d_i, F(n_0) ≡ 0 (mod k)} = k^{d_i}, since the constant term is determined by the other coefficients.
items.note: Standard facts. Together they produce the factor (φ(M)/M)^n in Lemma 4.7. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: CRT factorisation of sums over residue tuples
items.statement: Let W be square-free and, for each prime ℓ | W, let f_ℓ be a function on tuples R ∈ ((ℤ/ℓ)[t])^n with deg R_i ≤ d_i. Then Σ_{R ∈ ((ℤ/W)[t])^n, deg R_i ≤ d_i} ∏_{ℓ | W} f_ℓ(R mod ℓ) = ∏_{ℓ | W} Σ_{R ∈ ((ℤ/ℓ)[t])^n, deg R_i ≤ d_i} f_ℓ(R). The same holds under side conditions that are local at each ℓ, e.g. gcd(R_i(m), W) = 1, which means R_i(m) ≢ 0 mod ℓ for every ℓ | W.
items.locator: Published proofs of Lemma 4.6 p. 710 ('a standard argument based on the Chinese remainder theorem') and Lemma 4.9 p. 714 ('a factorisation argument')
items.note: Needed to pass from Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7 (one prime) to the modulus W. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: First moment of B_R over residues with unit values at m
items.statement: Let W = ∏_{ℓ∤M, ℓ≤log x} ℓ, m ∈ ℤ, all d_i ≥ 1 and d = Σd_i. Then Σ_{R ∈ ((ℤ/W)[t])^n, deg R_i ≤ d_i, gcd(R_i(m), W) = 1 for all i} B_R(x) = W^d φ(W)^n ∏_{ℓ | W} γ_n(ℓ).
items.note: Follows from the CRT factorisation and Lemma 2.7 (item 95). For each ℓ | W the local sum is ℓ^{d+n}γ_n(ℓ)(1 − ℓ^{−1})^{2n}/(1 − ℓ^{−1})^n = ℓ^dφ(ℓ)^nγ_n(ℓ). This identity is what shows that the prefactor printed on p. 713 must be W^dφ(W)^n (new misprint below). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Truncated second moment of the prime count (Eq. 4.5)
items.statement: For δ > 0 and 3 ≤ x ≤ (log H)^δ: Σ_{P ∈ ℤ[t]^n, |P| ≤ H, deg P_i = d_i, P_i > 0} θ^Λ_P(x)² = x²M^{n−2}φ(M)^{−n}2^dH^{d+n}∏_{ℓ∤M, ℓ≤log x}γ_n(ℓ) + O(x²H^{d+n}/log x + xH^{d+n}(log H)^n). The same right side bounds Σ_P θ_P(x)² from above.
items.note: From Lemma 4.4 (item 88) and Lemma 4.5 (item 42); x^{3/2} ≤ x²/log x. The paper prints it as an equality for θ_P (cf. E10). It is the first of the three moments used in §4.4 (item 47). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Most Schinzel tuples have a large prime count (Eq. 4.10)
items.statement: Assume gcd(∏Q_i(n_0), M) = 1 and fix A > 0. Put A_1 = n + A/2 and A_2 = n + 3A/4, and let β_0 be as in Lemma 4.11 (item 49). For all sufficiently large H and every x with (log H)^{A_1} < x < (log H)^{A_2}: #{P ∈ Poly(H): P Schinzel, θ_P(x) ≥ (β_0/2)(log log x)^{n−d}x} / #{P ∈ Poly(H): P Schinzel} = 1 + O((log log log H)^{d−n}(log log H)^{−1/2}).
items.locator: Published end of proof of Theorem 1.5, pp. 716–717, Eq. (4.10)
items.note: Proof: Lemma 4.10 (item 48) with ε(x) = (β_0/2)(log log x)^{n−d}, together with Lemma 4.11. Uses log x ≍ log log H and log log x = log log log H + O(1). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Few tuples of small height
items.statement: For H ≥ 1: #{P ∈ ℤ[t]^n: deg P_i = d_i, |P| ≤ H^{1/2}} ≪ H^{(n+d)/2} ≤ H^{n+d−1/2}. So all but O(H^{n+d−1/2}) of the n-tuples with |P| ≤ H have |P| > H^{1/2}.
items.note: Needed so that x ≤ (log H)^{A_2} ≤ (log|P|)^{n+A} for the remaining tuples. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Prime count bounded by the witness set
items.statement: Let P ∈ ℤ[t]^n with deg P_i = d_i, P_i > 0 and |P| ≤ H, let C > 0 and 1 ≤ x ≤ (log|P|)^C. Then θ_P(x) ≤ #S_C(P)·∏_{i=1}^n log((d_i+1)Hx^{d_i}). In particular, if |P| > H^{1/2}, x ≤ (log H)^{n+3A/4} and H ≫_{A,n} 1, then θ_P(x) ≪ #S_{n+A}(P)(log H)^n.
items.note: Holds because 0 < P_i(m) ≤ (d_i+1)Hm^{d_i} for 1 ≤ m ≤ x. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Smoothness of the norm family over V_ℚ
items.statement: U_ℚ is smooth over V_ℚ with geometrically integral fibres: each fibre N_{K/ℚ}(z) = c, c ≠ 0, is a torsor under the norm-one torus R^1_{K/ℚ}𝔾_m and is isomorphic to 𝔾_m^{r−1} over ℚ̄. Consequently U_ℚ is smooth, and g: U_ℚ → 𝔸^1_ℚ and h: U_ℚ → 𝔸^{d+1}_ℚ are smooth, being f followed by the smooth projections V_ℚ → 𝔸^1_ℚ and V_ℚ → 𝔸^{d+1}_ℚ.
items.locator: Published §5.1 p. 718 ('Note that U_ℚ is smooth over V_ℚ with geometrically integral fibres'); used in the proof of Lemma 5.2 p. 718
items.note: Stated without proof. The same holds for the product family of §5.2 and is used there implicitly (the 'analogue of Lemma 5.2'). Smoothness of the joint map f, not only of g and h, is what the corrected proof of Lemma 5.2 (E14) needs. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Smooth morphisms are open on p-adic points (cited)
items.statement: If φ: X → Y is a smooth morphism of ℚ_p-schemes of finite type, the induced map X(ℚ_p) → Y(ℚ_p) is open for the p-adic topology. In particular (Y = Spec ℚ_p), every ℚ_p-point of a smooth X has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open p-adic ball.
items.locator: Published proof of Lemma 5.2 p. 718, cited [21, p. 80] (B. Conrad, Weil and Grothendieck approaches to adelic points, Enseign. Math. 58 (2012))
items.note: Black box, a form of the p-adic implicit function theorem. It is applied to f (not only to g and h) in the corrected proof (E14), and to the open subset U(ℤ_p) for the integral version. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Integral form of Lemma 5.2
items.statement: Let p be a prime and N ∈ U(ℤ_p). There is a positive integer M such that if ν ∈ ℤ_p and m ∈ ℤ_p^{d+1} satisfy max(|ν − g(N)|_p, |m − h(N)|_p) ≤ p^{−M}, then U_{ν,m}(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅. The same holds for the product family of §5.2 with m ∈ ℤ_p^{d+n}. Consequently, in the proofs of Theorems 5.3 and 5.8, ℳ ∩ {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)} is the full set of Bouniakowsky polynomials (resp. Schinzel n-tuples) m ≡ m_0 (mod M); for Theorem 5.8, t_p = n_p also satisfies (5.2) by (5.4)–(5.6).
items.locator: Implicit in the proofs of Theorem 5.3 (pp. 719–720) and Theorem 5.8 (p. 723); stated for conic bundles in §6.3 p. 733, (6.9)
items.note: Not stated in §5 (see the new gap). Proof: U(ℤ_p) is an open neighbourhood of N in U(ℚ_p) and f is smooth, so f(U(ℤ_p)) contains a ball about f(N). Alternatively, for Galois K a p-adic unit that is a norm from (K⊗ℚ_p)^* ≅ L^g is N_{L/ℚ_p}(y) with y ∈ 𝒪_L^*, hence a norm from (𝒪_K⊗ℤ_p)^*. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Local constancy of invariants on the product family (the 'analogue of Lemma 5.2')
items.statement: In the setting of §5.2, with K/ℚ cyclic with character χ: for p ∈ S and N_p ∈ U(ℚ_p) there is a positive integer M_p such that if ν ∈ ℚ_p and m ∈ ℚ_p^{d+n} satisfy max(|ν − g(N_p)|_p, |m_i − h_i(N_p)|_p) ≤ p^{−M_p} for i = 1,…,n (5.4), then inv_p(χ,P_i(ν,m_i)) = inv_p(χ,P_i(g(N_p),h_i(N_p))) for each i. Hence inv_p(χ,∏_iP_i(ν,m_i)) = Σ_i inv_p(χ,P_i(ν,m_i)) = inv_p(χ,∏_iP_i(g(N_p),h_i(N_p))) = 0 (5.5), and in particular U_{ν,m}(ℚ_p) ≠ ∅.
items.note: Asserted without proof. It holds because a ↦ inv_p(χ,a) is a homomorphism ℚ_p^* → ℚ/ℤ trivial on the open subgroup (ℚ_p^*)^r, and each P_i(g(N_p),h_i(N_p)) ≠ 0. The final vanishing holds because ∏_iP_i(g(N_p),h_i(N_p)) = N_{K/ℚ}(z) is a local norm. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Compact Brauer-condition set Z and congruence decomposition of ℳ (Theorem 5.8)
items.statement: Let Z ⊂ ∏_{p∈S}U(ℤ_p) be the set of (N_p) with Σ_{p∈S} inv_p(χ,P_i(g(N_p),h_i(N_p))) = 0 for i = 1,…,n (5.6). Each left-hand side is a locally constant ℤ/r-valued function, so Z is closed, hence compact, and f(Z) is covered by finitely many congruence neighbourhoods (5.4) centred at points of Z. Condition (5.2) gives ℳ ⊂ h(Z), so by CRT ℳ = ∪_j ℳ_j, with ℳ_j the Schinzel n-tuples m ≡ m_0 (mod M), m_0 ∈ ℤ^{d+n}, M = ∏_{p∈S}p^{M_p}. There is n_0 ∈ ℤ with (∏_iP_i(n_0,m_{0,i}), M) = 1 such that for ν ≡ n_0 (mod M) and every m ∈ ℳ_j: Σ_{p∈S}inv_p(χ,P_i(ν,m_i)) = 0 for each i (5.7), and Σ_i inv_p(χ,P_i(ν,m_i)) = 0 for each p ∈ S (5.8).
items.note: This is the Theorem 5.8 analogue of item 56. That ℳ_j is the full congruence class needs integral-local-persistence (new gap). Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Global cyclic-algebra norm criterion (Hasse norm theorem for cyclic K)
items.statement: For K/ℚ cyclic with character χ and a ∈ ℚ^*, the class (χ,a) ∈ Br(ℚ) vanishes iff a ∈ N_{K/ℚ}(K^*). Together with (5.3): a is a global norm iff it is a local norm at every place of ℚ.
items.locator: Used at the end of the proof of Theorem 5.8 p. 724 ('so it is zero due to the exactness of (5.3). Thus … is a global norm'); cf. [20, §1.3.4]
items.note: Not stated in the paper; standard (H²(Gal(K/ℚ),K^*) ≅ Ĥ⁰ = ℚ^*/N(K^*)). Items 60 and 68 call it 'cyclic splitting'. It gives the global step from the local one recorded in item 59. Planned: the Tau Ceti ClassFieldTheory roadmap, Layer 13, plans the cyclic Hasse norm theorem and Kronecker–Weber.

items.name: Kronecker–Weber and splitting of primes ≡ 1 mod M (cited, classical)
items.statement: Every finite abelian extension F/ℚ is contained in ℚ(ζ_M) for some M ≥ 1. A prime p ≡ 1 (mod M) splits completely in ℚ(ζ_M), hence in every subfield of ℚ(ζ_M).
items.locator: Published proof of Theorem 5.7 p. 721 (also Introduction p. 675)
items.note: Black box, applied to F = K^(+). Planned: the Tau Ceti ClassFieldTheory roadmap, Layer 13, plans the cyclic Hasse norm theorem and Kronecker–Weber.

items.name: Theorem 5.3 is the case n = 1 of Theorem 5.8
items.statement: For n = 1, condition (5.2) holds automatically: if (t_p,z_p) ∈ U_m(ℤ_p) then P(t_p,m) = N_{K/ℚ}(z_p) is a local norm, so inv_p(χ,P(t_p,m)) = 0. Hence Theorem 5.3 is the special case n = 1 of Theorem 5.8.
items.note: Schinzel 1-tuples are exactly Bouniakowsky polynomials (p. 674–675), so the sets 𝒫 and ℳ agree. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Unramified Brauer group of U_m for cyclic K (cited, remark only)
items.statement: [19, Cor. 2.6(c)]: if K/ℚ is cyclic with character χ and each P_i(t,m_i) is irreducible, the unramified Brauer group of U_m is contained in the subgroup of Br(ℚ(U_m)) generated by Br(ℚ) and the classes (χ,P_i(t,m_i)), i = 1,…,n. Hence, under (5.2), U_m has an adelic point orthogonal to Br(X) for every smooth proper model X of U_m, so Br(X) does not obstruct the Hasse principle on X.
items.locator: Published Remark 5.4(2) p. 719 and Remark 5.9(2) pp. 722–723; cited [19, Cor. 2.6(c)], see also [58, Prop. 2.2(b),(d)]
items.note: Motivation only; not used in any proof. The irreducibility hypothesis is only written in the sentence after the one citing [19]. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Fields satisfying the hypothesis of Theorem 5.7
items.statement: If K is a totally imaginary abelian extension of ℚ of class number 1, then K = K^(1) = K^(+), so Theorem 5.7 applies (e.g. K = ℚ(√−1,√2)). If K is imaginary quadratic, K^(1) is abelian over ℚ iff the class group of K is an elementary abelian 2-group [40, Cor. VI.3.4].
items.locator: Published §5.1 p. 721 (the paragraph after the proof of Theorem 5.7)
items.note: A remark, referred to in the Introduction pp. 675–676. See the new misprint about the '47 biquadratic extensions'. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Hilbert-symbol criterion for local solubility of a diagonal conic
items.statement: For a prime p and a,b,c∈ℚ_p^*, the projective conic ax²+by²+cz²=0 has a ℚ_p-point if and only if the Hilbert symbol (−ac,−bc)_p equals 1.
items.locator: Published §6.2 p. 729 (cited: [54, Ch. III, §1], Serre, Cours d'arithmétique)
items.note: A black box the paper states. Together with the product formula, it gives the parity argument in Lemma 6.6. Planned: the Tau Ceti QuadraticFormInvariants roadmap, §6C, plans the Hilbert symbol, its norm criterion and its product formula.

items.name: Hilbert reciprocity (product formula)
items.statement: For a,b∈ℚ^*, (a,b)_v=1 for all but finitely many places v of ℚ, and ∏_v (a,b)_v=1. Hence a conic over ℚ fails to have points over ℚ_v at an even number of places v.
items.locator: Published proof of Lemma 6.6 p. 730 ('the product formula for the Hilbert symbol implies that r is even')
items.note: A black box, used and not stated. Item 77's note mentions it, but it has no item of its own. Planned: the Tau Ceti QuadraticFormInvariants roadmap, §6C, plans the Hilbert symbol, its norm criterion and its product formula.

items.name: Local solubility of the conic at good primes and at the p_ij
items.statement: Let p be an odd prime and u,v,w integers prime to p. (a) ux²+vy²+wz²=0 has a ℚ_p-point. (b) ux²+vy²+pwz²=0 has a ℚ_p-point iff (−uv/p)=1. Hence, under the hypotheses of Lemma 6.6: C(ℚ_p)≠∅ for every p∤2a₁a₂a₃∏p_ij; C(ℚ_{p_ij})≠∅ iff (−a_{i′}a_{i″}π_{i′}π_{i″}/p_ij)=1, where {i,i′,i″}={1,2,3}; and C(ℝ)≠∅ because the a_i are not all of the same sign.
items.locator: Published proof of Lemma 6.6 p. 730; also §6.3 p. 733 ('this fibre is a conic with good reduction')
items.note: The first displayed equivalence of the proof of Lemma 6.6 is asserted without derivation. It follows from the Hilbert-symbol formulae of [54, Ch. III]. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Quadratic reciprocity for distinct odd primes
items.statement: For distinct odd primes p,q: (p/q)(q/p)=(−1)^{(p−1)(q−1)/4}.
items.locator: Published proof of Proposition 6.7 p. 732 ('Using quadratic reciprocity and the identities π_i=π(S_i)π(S_i^c)')
items.note: A black box. Mathlib has it (legendreSym.quadratic_reciprocity, jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity). Library: available at the pinned Mathlib.

items.name: Heath-Brown's bilinear estimate for Jacobi symbols [35, Cor. 4]
items.statement: Let M,N be positive integers and a_n, b_m complex numbers with |a_n|,|b_m|≤1. Then for every ε>0, Σ_{m≤M, m odd} Σ_{n≤N} a_n b_m (n/m) ≪_ε (MN)^ε (MN^{1/2}+M^{1/2}N) = (MN)^{1+ε}(M^{−1/2}+N^{−1/2}).
items.locator: Published proof of Lemma 6.3 p. 726 (cited: Heath-Brown, Acta Arith. 72 (1995) 235–275, Cor. 4)
items.note: A black box. The form above is Heath-Brown's Corollary 4 as quoted in C. Wilson, 'General bilinear forms in the Jacobi symbol over hyperbolic regions', eq. (1.3). The original was behind a bot wall and was not consulted. Rescaling by max|a|·max|b| and using M^{−1/2}+N^{−1/2}≤2min(M,N)^{−1/2} gives the first sum in the proof of Lemma 6.3. The denominator runs over odd integers, which is why that proof splits off l=2. Note that for K,L≥1 the '+K' term of Lemma 6.3 is dominated by (KL)^{1+ε}min(K,L)^{−1/2}, so it is harmless. Missing: routed to route 6.

items.name: The sums T_{S,P}(x) and the expansion (6.5)
items.statement: For S=(S₁,S₂,S₃) with S_i⊂[n_i], not all S_i empty and not all S_i=[n_i]: T_{S,P}(x):=Σ_{m∈ℕ∩[1,x], m≡n₀ (mod M), P_ij(m) prime ∀i,j, P_ij(m)≠P_rs(m) if (i,j)≠(r,s)} ∏_{i=1}^3 (−a_{i′}a_{i″}∏_kP_{i′k}(m)∏_lP_{i″l}(m) / ∏_{j∈S_i}P_ij(m)) ∏_{j=1}^{n_i} log P_ij(m) (6.6). Under the hypotheses of Proposition 6.7, Lemma 6.6 gives C_P(x)=2^{1−n}θ̃_P(x)+2^{−n}Σ*_S T_{S,P}(x) (6.5).
items.note: Lemma 6.6 applies with p_ij=P_ij(m) because P_ij(m)≡Q_ij(n₀) (mod M) is prime to M, and 2a₁a₂a₃|M. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Average bound for T_{S,P} (claim (6.8))
items.statement: For all H≥3 and all x with (log H)^{2n}<x≤(log H)^{3n}, and every S in Σ*: (1/♯Poly(H)) Σ_{P∈Poly(H)} |T_{S,P}(x)| ≪ x^{3/4}. Proof: after quadratic reciprocity, T_{S,P}(x)=η_P(x;h,k) for suitable indices h≠k, bounded functions F₁,F₂,G (independent of P) and a sign. Here h lies in some S_{i′}^c and k∈S_i, which needs n₁,n₂>0. Then apply Proposition 6.5 with A₁=2n, A₂=3n.
items.note: The distinctness condition in T_{S,P} must also be absorbed into F₁,F₂,G. See the new gap recorded under sourceIssues. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: C_P is close to 2^{1−n}θ_P on average
items.statement: For H≥3 and (log H)^{2n}<x≤(log H)^{3n}: (1/♯Poly(H)) Σ_{P∈Poly(H)} |C_P(x)−2^{1−n}θ_P(x)| ≪ x^{3/4}. Hence ♯{P∈Poly(H): |C_P(x)−2^{1−n}θ_P(x)|>x^{4/5}} ≪ ♯Poly(H)(log H)^{−n/10}. Combined with (4.10) and Proposition 2.8, this gives C_P(x)>0 for 100% of Schinzel P≡Q (mod M).
items.note: Uses (6.5), (6.8) and (6.7); see E19 for the needed averaged form of (6.7). Using (4.10) with x up to (log H)^{3n} needs Lemma 4.10 with A₁=2n, A₂=3n. That is allowed, because (4.10) was derived for general n<A₁<A₂, and one x per H suffices. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Generic diagonal conic bundle family U→V
items.statement: With variables x_ij=(x_{ij0},…,x_{ijd_ij}) and P_ij(t,x_ij)=Σ_k x_{ijk}t^k: V⊂𝔸^{d+n+1}_ℤ is the open subscheme ∏_{i,j}P_ij(t,x_ij)≠0, and U⊂ℙ²_ℤ×𝔸^{d+n+1}_ℤ is given by (6.1) and ∏P_ij≠0. f:U→V is the projection to (t,x); g and h are the projections to t and to x. The fibre of h over m is U_m.
items.note: The analogue of the §5 family. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: p-adic compactness and neighbourhoods for the conic family
items.statement: For every prime p: f(U(ℤ_p))=f(U(ℚ_p))∩V(ℤ_p) is closed in the compact set V(ℤ_p), so ∏_{p∈S}h(U(ℤ_p)) is compact. For p∈S and N_p∈U(ℤ_p) there is M_p≥1 such that if ν∈ℤ_p and m∈ℤ_p^{d+n} satisfy max(|ν−g(N_p)|_p, |m−h(N_p)|_p)≤p^{−M_p}, then U_{ν,m}(ℤ_p)≠∅ (6.9). For p∉S, the fibre of f at any ℤ_p-point of V has a ℚ_p-point.
items.note: Depends on the analogue of Lemma 5.2 and on [21, p. 79]. 9), which is repeated here. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Proper morphisms are topologically proper on ℚ_p-points [21, p. 79]
items.statement: If f: X→Y is a proper morphism of schemes of finite type over ℚ_p, then f: X(ℚ_p)→Y(ℚ_p) is a proper map of topological spaces. Since Y(ℚ_p) is locally compact Hausdorff, it is a closed map.
items.locator: Published §6.3 p. 733 (cited: Conrad, Enseign. Math. 58 (2012), p. 79)
items.note: A black box. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Reduction of Theorem 6.1 to one congruence class
items.statement: Finitely many balls ∏_{p∈S}𝓑_{N_p} cover ∏_{p∈S}h(U(ℤ_p)), so ℳ=∪_iℳ_i. For one ball, put n_p=g(N_p), m_p=h(N_p), M=∏_{p∈S}p^{M_p}, and choose n₀∈ℤ, m₀∈ℤ^{d+n} by CRT with n₀≡n_p, m₀≡m_p (mod p^{M_p}). Then ℳ_i={m∈𝒫: m≡m₀ (mod M)}, P_ij(n₀,m₀) is prime to M, and Proposition 6.7 applies with Q_ij(t)=P_ij(t,m₀).
items.note: Also needs 8a₁a₂a₃|M, which is not checked in the paper (new gap). Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Normalisation of the coefficients a_i (§6.4)
items.statement: (i) Replacing (a₁,P_{1,1}) by (−a₁,−P_{1,1}) leaves (6.1) unchanged, and is a height-preserving bijection on degree-d_{11} polynomials. So one may assume a₁,a₂,a₃ are not all of the same sign. (ii) If p²|a_i, replace a_i by a_i/p² and rescale the corresponding variable. If p divides two of the a_i, multiply (6.1) by p, divide those two a_i by p, multiply the third by p, and rescale; iterate. Neither step changes whether U_m(ℚ)≠∅, and after finitely many steps a₁a₂a₃ is square-free.
items.note: Checked: after removing squares, each prime has valuation 0 or 1 in each a_i. When two or three of them are 1, multiplying by p lowers the total valuation, and a final square removal finishes. The positive-leading-coefficient condition in Theorem 6.1 applies after the sign change, consistent with item 82's warning. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Reduction of Theorem 7.1 to R_d(H)
items.statement: For every d≥2, ε>0 and all sufficiently large H: ♯{f∈P_d(H): x²+y²=f(t) is soluble in ℤ}/♯P_d(H) ≥ R_d(H)−ε. Proof: apply Theorem 1.2 with n=1, M=4, n₀∈{0,1,2,3} and each Q₁ with Q₁(n₀)≡1 (mod 4). This gives m≡n₀ (mod 4) with f(m) prime, hence ≡1 (mod 4), hence a sum of two squares.
items.note: Uses Theorem 1.2 and Fermat's two-square theorem (item 85) as black boxes. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Limit of R_d(H)
items.statement: ♯P_d(H)∼2^dH^{d+1}, and lim_{H→∞}R_d(H)=r_d∏_{p≥3}(1−p^{−min{p,d+1}}). Here R_d(H)♯P_d(H)=Σ_{Q∈(ℤ/4)[t], deg Q≤d, ∃n₀: Q(n₀)≡1 (mod 4)} ♯{f∈P_d(H): f≡Q (mod 4), Z_f(p)≠p ∀p≥3}.
items.note: The partition identity is exact: the paper's 'Bouniakowsky' does not include irreducibility (p. 674), and the ℓ=2 condition follows from f(n₀)≡1 (mod 4). The local factor p^{−min(p,d+1)} is the proportion of polynomials of degree ≤d over 𝔽_p that vanish on all of 𝔽_p. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Values of the Euler product in Theorem 7.1
items.note: Stated without proof. Checked numerically: c₂=0.950751, c₃=0.960896, limit 0.962654. Corollary 7.2 follows from c₂>19/20, since (19/32)(19/20)=0.5641>0.56 (item 87). Missing: routed to route 1.

routes.title: Arithmetic statistics, counting fields and Selmer distributions, Part II: Schinzel averages over coefficient boxes
routes.reason: ST.0–5 provide height-family and number-field/Selmer counting infrastructure, but not positive-prime values of fixed-degree integer polynomials in growing coefficient boxes. This is different from the previously proposed growing-degree random-irreducibility direction. The local evaluation laws and three matched dispersion moments require new layers, importing generic family density and Fourier/arithmetic suppliers.
routes.brief: Extend Arithmetic statistics, counting fields and Selmer distributions (ArithmeticStatistics). Import ST.0 relative height-family density; Sieve methods, prime gaps and prime patterns (SieveMethodsAndPrimePatterns) for quadratic-character bilinear input; Exponential sums, decoupling and the circle method (ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod) for kernel estimates; Analytic number theory, zeta functions and prime distribution (AnalyticNumberTheory) for Möbius, Mertens, PNT and multiplicative means. Endpoint contracts are items 9,11–15,24–25,74,79 and 83–84. In particular for fixed positive degrees d_i and M, n<A₁<A₂ and log^{A₁}H<x≤log^{A₂}H, the desired average absolute discrepancy is O(x/√log x); for Schinzel tuples in compatible congruence classes the fraction with at least (log|P|)^{A/3} prime witnesses up to (log|P|)^{n+A} is 1+O((logloglogH)^{D−n}/√loglog H). Preserve the common input, positive primes, positive leading coefficients, coefficientwise congruence and exact normalization. Use the even von Mangoldt function on ℤ (item 28): Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.8 and Lemma 3.9 hold for it, and Lemma 3.14 holds in its von Mangoldt form (item 34), not for positive primes alone (E1). Run the dispersion for θ^Λ (item 100) and pass to positive primes with a bound the paper does not state but which holds: the mean over the box of θ^Λ_P(x) − θ_P(x) is ≪ (log H)^n log x; this uses n < A₁. State Corollary 1.10 pointwise in x (item 15). Construct finite-field coefficient probability, Vandermonde fibers, G_p, c_p, γ_n, singular series, CRT counting, large-prime tails and weighted counts with the stated API/tests. Reuse the built Vandermonde and natural Mangoldt APIs. Distinct-prime claims require deleting the repeated-polynomial diagonals. Proposed files: TauCeti/NumberTheory/PolynomialPrimeValues/LocalModels.lean and Dispersion.lean. Import the Bouniakowsky and Schinzel predicates (items 3, 4) from SieveMethodsAndPrimePatterns:SV.4. Proposed landmarks: Bernoulli Euler factors; Schinzel on average; quadratic-character cancellation. No conjectural full Schinzel or fixed-polynomial Bateman–Horn theorem is a proved endpoint. Corrections the design must carry: Lemma 3.14 as printed counts only positive prime values and is false; the main term needs the von Mangoldt function read evenly on ℤ (E1), and Theorem 3.1 likewise needs Λ extended evenly to the negative integers (E4); Lemmas 4.1 and 4.4 and (4.5) inherit the one-sided proof (E10); Lemma 4.9 is false for θ_P and holds for θ^Λ, which is enough for Theorem 1.9 since A₁ > n (E30); Corollary 1.10 needs one exceptional set valid for all x at once, which the paper does not supply (E11); and (6.7) must exclude tuples with a repeated polynomial, which form a negligible proportion (E19).

routes.title: Heights, rational points and obstructions, Part II: random norm and conic fibrations
routes.reason: RP.2–3 own Brauer evaluation and descent, not density-one existence theorems across arbitrary-degree coefficient families. Add their arithmetic-family applications as new layers. Do not rebuild class field theory, Hasse–Minkowski, generic scheme carriers or the prime-value engine.
routes.brief: Extend Heights, rational points and obstructions (HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions), importing RP.2 cyclic norm obstruction APIs and ArithmeticStatisticsPartIISchinzelAverages for fixed-degree prime-value statistics. Import Class field theory (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ClassFieldTheory), layers 5,6,10,12, for local invariants, unramified norm units, ABHN and strict ray-class splitting, and Global quadratic forms (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GlobalQuadraticForms), layer 5, for Hasse–Minkowski. Endpoint 61 is relative density 1 of rational points among cyclic norm fibers satisfying the specified unit-integral local conditions at ramified primes, together with positive ambient coefficient density. Endpoint 67 retains the column-sum Brauer conditions for a product of generic polynomials. Endpoint 65 gives a positive proportion of integral affine norm equations only under the additional hypothesis K^(+)/Q abelian. Endpoints 80–82 give relative density 1 of locally unit-soluble diagonal conic bundles and positive ambient proportion for arbitrary nonzero diagonal coefficients, with n₁,n₂>0,n₃≥0 and all prescribed polynomial degrees positive; resulting points lie in smooth fibers. Endpoints 86–87 give the exact product lower bound and >56% for x²+y²=P(t), d≥2. They use the prime-value input of the Schinzel-averages Part II, with the repair recorded there (E1, E4). Build basis-independent integral norm forms, unit-open universal families, joint smooth local persistence, compact-image finite CRT covers, invariant matrices, character indicators and thin-diagonal removal. Preserve the distinction between affine integral solutions and integral points of the unit-open scheme. The real sign hypothesis and nonzero projective vector must be explicit. Suggested files: TauCeti/ArithmeticGeometry/RandomFibrations/Norm.lean and Conic.lean. Suggested landmarks: local congruence cover; random cyclic norm Hasse principle; conic-solubility indicator;56percent integral Châtelet bound. No unrestricted Brauer–Manin completeness is asserted. Corrections the design must carry: in Lemma 5.2 the joint map (g, h) is open because f is smooth, not because g and h are (E14); the proofs of Theorems 5.3 and 5.8 need ℤ_p-points on the fibres, not only ℚ_p-points, which holds for cyclic K by a short norm argument (E32); in §6.3 the modulus must be a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃ (E40), local points on the family must be exhibited for the positive-density claim (E41), and the distinctness of prime values must be carried into T_{S,P} (E37); and the proof of Corollary 1.7 works only when a is not a square, since for square a Holzer's solution has z = 0 (E24).

routes.reason: The generic relative coefficient-height density interface belongs to ST.0. This paper supplies essential denominator tests and congruence-subfamily uses; its specific prime-value law is a separate PartII consumer.

AN.5 owns Möbius cancellation, uniform multiplicative means and Euler-product estimates; AN.2 supplies their quantitative prime-distribution prerequisites. The truncated/signed Mangoldt interface reuses the existing natural ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt, exposing what is genuinely missing rather than duplicating it. Original proof extraction is still required.

The symmetric and one-sided Dirichlet-kernel L1 bounds are reusable oscillatory-sum inputs, with the one-sided case needed to repair the degree 1 coefficient calculation. The random-polynomial specialization stays in its PartII.

Heath-Brown's quadratic-character bilinear estimate belongs to the existing large-sieve/bilinear-sum layer. The prime-denominator 2 error and exact norms must be retained; a generic DFT or character-orthogonality theorem does not establish this bound.

RP.2 owns effective Brauer evaluation and local-to-global obstruction tests. Add the cyclic norm class and invariant-matrix adapters here, importing the CFT local invariant and ABHN sequence without re-planning them. The density-one geometric applications consume these interfaces in the PartII.

SV.4 already receives Schinzel's Hypothesis (H) from PAPER-HARPAZ-WITTENBERG-16/72, whose hypothesis is this admissibility condition (positive leading coefficients, no fixed prime divisor of the product). Define the Bouniakowsky and Schinzel predicates once there; the Schinzel-averages Part II imports them.

The Proposition 6.7 p. 730 occurrence ('a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃', where 0 is a multiple) is outside my range, but the same convention argument applies. In all three places M is used only as a modulus ('m ≡ n₀ (mod M)', 'P ≡ Q (mod M)', 'coprime to M'). A modulus is read as a positive integer by the standard convention of analytic number theory. Negative M is harmless, since mod M means mod |M|. The paper states the positivity wherever it is used quantitatively: Theorem 1.9 ('n, d_1,…,d_n, M be positive integers', p. 680), from which Theorems 1.5 and 1.2 are derived; Definition 1.8 (M ∈ ℕ, with φ(M) and M^{1−n}); Corollary 1.6; Proposition 2.8; Corollary 2.9. Here ℕ = {1,2,…} (p. 684: 'd_1,…,d_n ∈ ℕ', used on p. 685 as 'd_i ⩾ 1'). The ledger's counterexample for Theorem 1.2 (M = 0, n₀ = 0, Q = t+1) is literally valid, but only under the degenerate reading 'congruence modulo 0 = equality', which no reader would adopt there. For Proposition 6.7, M = 0 does not even give a counterexample. P ≡ Q (mod 0) forces P = Q, and m ≡ n₀ (mod 0) forces m = n₀. (Q_ij(n₀), 0) = 1 forces Q_ij(n₀) = ±1, so the fibre at n₀ is a smooth conic. Every prime divides 0, so the hypothesis gives local points at every prime, hence at ℝ by Hilbert reciprocity. The first reading's proposed rejection is correct.
